article.title: Beyond the Blue Wave
article.author: Michael Albert
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. To reject fascism is a necessary and good thing. The 2026 election results are part of that. But we should also acknowledge a sad reality. We have not overnight entered another better world. To joyously celebrate having elected some new and quite promising Democrats, some other typical business-as-usual Democrats, and especially to have the Democrats as a whole re-empowered is fully warranted. Glass half full says Trumpism is on the way out. Trump will be but another stain, albeit a major one, on a long-since and repeatedly horribly re-stained history. But Trump will not redirect history to become forever worse. Fascism is stopped. We needed that. Trump is trounced. We celebrate that. Glass half empty says we are celebrating lesser enemies of the people re-empowered, not people’s emissaries finally triumphant. To have lived sixty years after having decided with my generation that my society needed comprehensive revolution, and to be watching election returns, and to smile because the Democratic Party has gotten back in the saddle—yes, it is what we immediately needed, but no it is very far from what we ultimately want. We understandably joyously celebrate tentative survivalism having struck a blow against vicious exterminism. We joyously welcome back into the societal saddle the less vile capitalist, sexist, racist, authoritarianism that birthed the even more vile Trumpism. We celebrate for a day and maybe even for two or three days. It was an essential step. But when we realize the actual character of what we are celebrating, then what? Will we relax? Electorally sated? Or will we escalate our demands and invigorate our energies? Related: Upsurges Bubble Around the Globe but Will it Evolve into Effective Change? Look ahead. It is always problematic to do so. After all, what can we confidently say about a better future? Nonetheless, look ahead. It is often essential to do so. What must we cautiously say about a better future if we are to sensibly seek it? People voted against Donald but if we look a little deeper we see that many people changed their views to do so. Many people didn’t just reject Donald, they reversed prior commitments. And neither Trump’s lies and threats nor, even more instructive, big donor massive money could fully block that. Not could MAGA identity. Does anyone think it was a “we love the Democratic Party” sentiment at work? No, the day’s message was we want real change and we are starting to understand what real change can really mean. To continue that trend we need to now fight to scuttle tariff stupidity. To cancel hyperscaler data centers. To reinstate Trump-terminated social programs. To expand health care. To address atrophying infrastructure. To amply finance education and teachers. To abolish ICE. To re-elevate feminism. To pursue a national wealth tax that precludes billionaires running to escape it. To end the war. To slash the military budget. To impeach Trump, Hegseth, and RFK Jr., and to prosecute corruption. And as wild as all that would be, look closely, it is actually virtually all already popularly desired. But let’s also look ahead. Let’s guess that the upcoming Presidential primary season causes more people to change their views. Let’s hypothesize that 2028 pits AOC against some troglodyte Republican in a race to claim the Oval Office. In that case, what should a serious, committed, anti-authoritarian, feminist, anti-racist, anti-capitalist organization or individual do? And what should that same organization or individual do beyond the next election? To address those questions we should’ve consider what will need to be done and who will be available and even eager to do it. Zohran Mamdani enlisted 90,000 volunteers to become Mayor of New York City. Mamdani won. He is now Mayor. He must now win gains for deserving constituencies while he navigates the pressures of keeping the city functional. At the same time, New York will live on after his tenure. So regarding the city’s future, popular movements need to further raise public consciousness, further galvanize urban energies, further inspire activist constituencies to establish longer run structures, undertake extensive campaigns, and discover and share visionary aims to further pursue. Related: Trump Needs “Good Americans” to Look the Other Way The national situation that AOC or any other progressive candidate who wins the Presidency in 2028 would face will be similar but even more conflicted, diverse, and chaotic than Mamdani’s situation in New York. Yet to win the Oval Office, despite its larger scale and greater stakes, will encounter at least the same two big agenda tasks. Task1: Positively navigate the exigencies of first winning the office and of then governing in the election’s aftermath. And simultaneously, Task 2: Positively establish organizational and programmatic means to arouse diverse constituencies to persistently pursue wider, deeper vision. Electorally win office. Govern. Implement immediate gains. Simultaneously, extra-electorally build activist means and cultivate activist desires to win more and larger gains later. Does any radical much less any revolutionary disagree? If not, is there more we can usefully say? One overarching movement issue we face is that Task 1, which is to deal with winning the Oval Office and to maintain services and meet immediate needs, typically falls short of assisting and can even become incompatible with Task 2 which needs winning and maintenance to deal with present needs in ways that become compatible with and support activism to develop more comprehensive vision and practice for the future. So a progressive electoral project will need to seek needed improvements and maintain and administer systems in 2029, but also to intersect supportively with a parallel activist extra electoral project to transform underlying institutions to create a fundamentally better future? When Hugo Chavez, undeniably charismatic and capable, won presidential power in Venezuela, what happened? Down the road, way less happened than what he and the masses of Chavistas hoped for. Was that just tough luck or did things go wrong that could be corrected in another time and another place? When Chavez became Venezuela’s President, there was one leftist governor, no leftist police departments, and maybe two or three leftist mayors on his side and beyond that there were residual troglodytes and intensely aggressive antagonistic business exploiters and media manipulators who profoundly hated him and his supporters. There were also, throughout Venezuela, many culturally and socially regressive holdover habits. And there was a multiply divided population. A victorious progressive AOC, or whoever might emerge from a wildly successful 2028 election would be in a similar but still worse situation than Chavez endured because where Chavez started with strong support in the military AOC would not likely have that. And where Chavez had the U.S. government and corporate elites as an enemy without—AOC would have that enemy operating from within. So what emerges from considering a still hypothetical electoral project two years before 2028? Those with eyes wide open, or even with eyes not thoroughly occluded, would in this scenario surely vote for AOC. Look at today’s returns. Texas, Michigan, Kansas, and more switched big at every level. Add two more years of Trump. Get way more youth involved like Mamdani did. You can imagine it if you try. Best case, not 90,000 but millions of volunteers open still more eyes to build the massive momentum needed to carry AOC to victory. She and her team and the broad public would, in that best case, induce the needed momentum for that to happen—like Mamdani and his team and supporters induced the needed momentum in NYC. That will be Task 1 mentioned earlier. That will win and then administer. But if we suppose that is attainable, and if we hypothesize it occurs for this possible future, then what about Task 2? What would pressure the new administration from without on behalf of developing further vision and arousing new confidence, desires, and lasting structures able to continue escalating progress year after year until fundamental victory? The aim wouldn’t be to win office and the movement then dissipates. The aim would be to win office and the movement then persists, expands, deepens, and finally wins a fundamentally reconstructed country. Who will prioritize achieving that? Related: From the New Left to Trump: Why Movements of the 1960s Failed to Build Lasting Power And so we come to the choices DSA and other grass roots individuals and local and national progressive and revolutionary organizations will face starting roughly a year from now, and perhaps even sooner—indeed maybe even this week. Whatever specific answers emerge, undoubtedly many nuances and details will arise from new lessons gained and from new conditions that arise as energetic efforts unfold. But even with all that indeterminacy, is there anything we can say now about how to arrive at wise choices able to incorporate new lessons and productively address unfolding conditions? One path is that we ask what needs doing. A partial answer could be that Task 1 and Task 2 need doing. Then we might also ask who will do what is needed, and derivatively, finally, we might ask where will our efforts do the most good? Isn’t that a worthy approach not only for an organization like DSA to decide its role, but also for individuals including writers, activists and organizers to decide theirs? The idea would be determine what is needed and to then decide among all that is needed what we are able to do well, and especially what is otherwise unlikely to be done as well or even just sufficiently if we don’t help do it. The idea would be to do that which we can do that will have the greatest positive desirable impact we can have. Consider DSA engaging with an AOC versus some vile thug election. One observation we might arrive at would be that by virtue of its collective talents and already displayed capacities DSA could certainly attract votes to help AOC win and then help with ideas, volunteers, and staff to administer government. Another observation we might arrive at would be that DSA could productively work to develop vision, infrastructure, and extra-electoral campaigns to raise means and consciousness extending beyond present-day administration to seek future fundamental change. Weighing circumstances, one conclusion as events proceed might be that while DSA could contribute to Task 1 by helping to amass votes needed to win, and could then help conceive steps to win immediate gains, to contribute those efforts would not be particularly decisive. Other actors, less radically aware and less experienced could do those same things. If an AOC campaign was going to win, the energy and insights to accomplish those steps might arise overwhelmingly from previously inexperienced volunteers to such a degree that contributions from long-term more committed and experienced activists and organizations would be at most peripheral. On the other hand, to build momentum for grassroots consciousness raising and to initiate activist campaigns able to push the new administration to build infrastructure and prepare its supporters to seek more and larger gains might fundamentally depend on and reflect efforts by more established actors and so might be where DSA involvement would have most impact on long-term success. Of course, the conclusion could also possibly be the reverse, that just to win requires all hands and all thoughts and all efforts narrowly and immediately applied to, well, just winning. What’s my point? It is that the calculation of what to do is not mainly about what appeals to us. It is not mainly about what feels good for us. And it is not mainly about what displays the most militancy. It is about evaluating what is most needed and who and what can achieve it. It is about exerting energy where one’s efforts will have the most beneficial consequences. It requires a careful accounting of available means, a look-ahead to outcomes needed, and an assessment of the predictable consequences of one’s choices among possible options for what to do. Related: Navigating These Times What if one sees a fuzzy picture? What if there isn’t one single path that nearly everyone in DSA, for example, can agree is best? Then a new choice arises. To vote for one path and require that all members follow it. Or to see more than one advocated way forward and decide to respect different strokes for different folks though with all those involved seeking the same ultimate goal even while pursuing different steps toward it. In other words to decide to acknowledge and respect differences and welcome diversity. So, a group like DSA might agree on the aim, for example to help accomplish Task 1 and Task 2, but respect members who favor two or more ways for its chapters and members to contribute to attaining the aim. Members debate. Partisans of each path respect partisans of the other path. Both paths proceed. Experience evaluates. Znetwork
